cards.title: Constant-factor Π₂ hardness of approximating linear discrepancy
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Historical conjecture, resolved affirmatively: is there an absolute constant γ>1 such that distinguishing lindisc(A)≤t from lindisc(A)>γt is Π₂^P-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, given a rational m×n matrix A and a positive rational threshold t? Here lindisc(A)=max_{w∈[0,1]ⁿ} min_{x∈{0,1}ⁿ} ‖A(w−x)‖∞. Manurangsi’s published theorem establishes the requested hardness for every fixed γ=9/8−ε with 0<ε<1/8. The source’s damaged fraction 32 referred to a 3/2 covering-radius comparison; its conjecture asks for analogous constant-factor hardness of linear discrepancy, not explicitly the identical 3/2 factor.
cards.why: Establishes that approximating the worst-case error of binary rounding captures the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy, beyond ordinary NP-hardness.
cards.status_note: Matched the original conjecture to Manurangsi’s Theorem 1 and the complete Lemma 5 reduction statement. Verified the journal publication metadata and read the September 2026 follow-up’s model and theorem. Resolution concerns some constant-factor Π₂ hardness, as explicitly claimed by the direct follow-up; no independent proof audit or proof-assistant certificate is claimed.

cards.definitions: The matrix entries and t are encoded as binary rational numerators and positive denominators; both dimensions are part of the input and unbounded. For y∈Rᵐ, ‖y‖∞=max_{j∈[m]}|y_j|. A fractional vector w ranges over the entire real cube [0,1]ⁿ and x is a binary rounding of all its coordinates. Thus the maximization is outside the minimization: a different x may be chosen for each w. The maximum exists because the minimum of finitely many continuous functions of w is continuous on a compact set. This is not discrepancy at just w=(1/2,…,1/2), and the rounding vector does not range over all integer vectors as in lattice covering radius. The promise problem accepts instances with lindisc(A)≤t and rejects those with lindisc(A)>γt; behavior in the intervening gap is unrestricted. Π₂^P consists of languages decidable by a polynomial-time predicate with one polynomial-length universal binary quantifier followed by one polynomial-length existential binary quantifier. Hardness means that every language in this class has a deterministic polynomial-time map taking its yes instances into the low-discrepancy case and its no instances into the high-discrepancy case. The factor γ is fixed before the reduction and does not depend on the matrix dimensions. A γ-approximation to the value in the one-sided convention returns v with lindisc(A)≤v≤γ lindisc(A); the gap statement avoids ambiguity about approximation conventions.
cards.answer_criterion: The published Π₂ reduction resolves the constant-factor hardness conjecture: it has lindisc(A)≤4/3 in the yes case and lindisc(A)≥3/2 in the no case, giving hardness at every factor strictly below 9/8. This is an unconditional hardness theorem, not an unconditional proof that no polynomial-time algorithm exists. It does not establish hardness at factor 3/2, and no such stronger target is substituted for the source’s general conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Worst-case rounding error is the quantity being approximated
context_blocks.text: Linear discrepancy measures the largest, over fractional vectors, of the smallest achievable row-wise rounding error. Finding a useful rounding for one given vector and estimating this worst-case value are different computational tasks.

context_blocks.title: The source’s hardness question had a later direct answer

They conjectured analogous constant-factor Π₂ approximation hardness to the lattice covering-radius problem. Manurangsi’s 2021 theorem explicitly answers that question.

context_blocks.title: The numerical factors belong to different problems

Its reduction has thresholds 4/3 and 3/2, whose ratio is 9/8; the occurrence of 3/2 as an absolute no-case threshold must not be mistaken for that approximation ratio.

cards.context:
Linear discrepancy measures the largest, over fractional vectors, of the smallest achievable row-wise rounding error. Finding a useful rounding for one given vector and estimating this worst-case value are different computational tasks.

Li and Nikolov proved NP-hardness of exact evaluation and membership of the rational threshold problem in Π₂. They conjectured analogous constant-factor Π₂ approximation hardness to the lattice covering-radius problem. Manurangsi’s 2021 theorem explicitly answers that question.

The source compares with a 3/2 covering-radius hardness result. The direct linear-discrepancy follow-up supplies a 9/8−ε factor. Its reduction has thresholds 4/3 and 3/2, whose ratio is 9/8; the occurrence of 3/2 as an absolute no-case threshold must not be mistaken for that approximation ratio.

Bennett and Ly cite Manurangsi’s published Π₂ hardness for ℓ∞ linear discrepancy and extend it to a binary covering-radius promise problem. Their work also studies finite ℓp norms. This is later progress beyond a question already settled in 2021.

cards.formal: Historical Question 1: can either VC dimension or Littlestone dimension of an explicitly listed finite Boolean concept class be approximated within some fixed constant factor in polynomial time? Under randomized ETH, the answer is negative for each dimension, already by Theorem 2 of the cited paper. “Either” allows choosing one dimension once; it does not require one algorithm to estimate both simultaneously.

cards.definitions:
The input lists a finite domain \(X\) and a nonempty finite class \(\mathcal C\) of Boolean functions on \(X\), by its full binary incidence matrix \(M_{x,c}=c(x)\). The target is not given by a succinct circuit or by a sampling oracle. Domain size and number of listed concepts both vary with the input; duplicate concept columns may be removed. Let \(L\) denote the total explicit encoding length, with \(L\geq2\) for asymptotic notation.

The VC dimension is the largest integer \(d\geq0\) for which some set \(S\subseteq X\) of size \(d\) is shattered: every function \(S\to\{0,1\}\) occurs as the restriction of a concept in \(\mathcal C\).

For Littlestone dimension, consider a deterministic online learner with no computational restriction. On each round it receives \(x_{t}\in X\), predicts a bit, then learns the true bit \(y_{t}\). The finite sequence is realizable when a single concept \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(x_{t})=y_{t}\) on every round. The learner's mistake bound is the maximum number of wrong predictions over all realizable sequences of any finite length. Littlestone dimension is the minimum such bound over all learners.

Equivalently, Littlestone dimension is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree whose internal nodes are labeled by elements of \(X\), whose outgoing edges have labels \(0,1\), and for which every root-to-leaf sequence of examples and edge labels is realized by some concept. The concept may differ between paths. These are combinatorial definitions of the number being estimated; constructing an approximately optimal online learner is a separate algorithmic problem.

Fix one of the two dimensions and write its value as \(D\). A constant-factor approximation means that there is a fixed \(r\geq1\), independent of the matrix dimensions and input, and a uniform polynomial-time algorithm outputting a binary-encoded rational \(\widehat D\) with
\[D/r\leq\widehat D\leq D.\]
For a randomized algorithm, this must hold with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. Time is polynomial in \(L\) in the worst case. No shattered set or online strategy must accompany the numerical estimate. When \(D=0\), successful approximation requires output zero.

Randomized ETH, the assumption used here, asserts that no randomized \(2^{o(N)}\)-time algorithm decides satisfiability of all \(N\)-variable 3CNF formulas with bounded error. Polynomial dependence on the explicit formula length is allowed; repetitions can be removed so that its size is polynomial in \(N\). The paper's Section 2.2 expressly treats reductions and the associated hypothesis as randomized. A deterministic-only version of ETH is not silently substituted.

The conditional negative result rules out every fixed factor \(r\), including large constants, for each of the dimensions separately. It is not an unconditional lower bound, and it is not merely hardness of finding the exact integer value.
cards.answer_criterion: The source already proves the negative answer under randomized ETH. A positive constant-factor polynomial-time algorithm for either dimension would contradict that assumption. The historical question is therefore recorded as conditionally resolved rather than as an unreviewed open challenge; no unconditional nonexistence assertion is made.

cards.context:
Question 1 appears in the introduction to motivate the paper. Theorem 2 rules out constant-factor approximation under randomized ETH, and other theorems establish stronger guarantees under stronger or alternative hypotheses.

For a nonempty class with \(m\) distinct concepts, both dimensions are at most \(\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor\). Zero-dimensional cases can be recognized directly, and outputting one on the remaining cases gives an \(O(\log L)\)-factor estimate. Thus a coarse logarithmic approximation does not supply an arbitrary fixed constant factor.

Theorem 2 excludes polynomial-time approximation within \(o(\log L/(\log\log L)^{\xi})\) for some constant \(\xi>0\), under randomized ETH. Under the paper’s randomized Gap-ETH or Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, Theorems 3 and 4 strengthen this to \(o(\log L)\). Those extra hypotheses are not needed for the constant-factor negative answer.

The conclusion notes that computing a near-optimal mistake-bound number is not known to be equivalent to constructing an efficient online learner with a near-optimal mistake bound. This unresolved approximate-strategy question is not substituted for the extracted numerical approximation task.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
